title: Short Stuff: Tulipmania
summary: Short Stuff episode on Tulipmania, the 1630s Dutch tulip bulb speculative bubble. Hosts explain what an economic bubble is (rapid price rise driven by exuberant trading and speculation, then a panic-driven crash), then trace how tulips arrived in Holland around 1600 via the Dutch East India Company, became a status symbol after 1634, and were priced at extreme levels (2,000 florin per bulb, with comparisons to cheese, beer, sheep and oxen). Speculation through futures contracts traded on the Dutch stock exchange drew in people of all classes, and the bubble burst less than two years after it began in 1636, ruining buyers and suppliers. Courts treated the contracts as non-binding bets, and a settlement at ten percent of face value satisfied no one. The Dutch economy took decades to recover. The episode closes with the Dutch still paying premium prices for tulip bulbs, a Conan O'Brien bit on Amsterdam tulip farms, and a recommendation to plant tulips.

segments.title: Opening and defining an economic bubble
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce Tulip Mania as perhaps the first financial bubble and explain how a bubble inflates through exuberant trading and then bursts, leaving late holders with worthless assets.

segments.title: Tulips arrive in Holland
segments.summary: Chuck describes the wild tulip origins in Central Asia and the Himalayas. Josh explains tulips reached Holland around 1600 via the Dutch East India Company, were a niche collector's plant for decades, and became a status symbol among the nobility in 1634.

segments.title: Extreme tulip bulb prices
segments.summary: Chuck explains demand from wealthy buyers pushed prices through the roof. A single bulb could fetch 2,000 florin, equal to 16,000 pounds of cheese, 250 tons of beer, or a few hundred sheep, which the hosts convert to tens of thousands to a million dollars for rare bulbs.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break between segments, with the hosts returning from the break.

segments.title: Speculation and futures contracts
segments.summary: Josh describes wealthy buyers growing tulips as status displays, then people speculating by buying to resell and by trading futures contracts on future bulb sales. Speculation is named as a key driver of the bubble.

segments.title: Spread of the frenzy and the crash
segments.summary: Chuck says the Dutch stock exchange traded the bulbs and that people of all classes sold homes and tools to invest. The bubble burst less than two years after the frenzy began in 1636. Josh explains that as holders rushed to sell, panic triggered a precipitous price drop that ruined those holding large stocks.

segments.title: Fallout for buyers, suppliers and the Dutch economy
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that buyers who owed large sums on futures contracts could not pay suppliers. Courts refused to hear the cases because bets were not legally binding. A settlement at ten percent of contract value satisfied no one, and the government ultimately did nothing, leaving the economy to recover over decades.

segments.title: Dutch tulip legacy and Conan O'Brien recommendation
segments.summary: Josh notes the Dutch still pay premium prices for tulip bulbs and the countryside blooms each spring. Chuck recommends a Conan O'Brien bit filmed at Amsterdam tulip farms and markets.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck recommends planting tulips and Josh offers a closing warning about economic bubbles.
